concepts.name: Claims versus opinions
concepts.summary: Recognise that a claim is a statement that can be true or false, and distinguish factual claims from value judgments and preferences.

concepts.name: Indicator words
concepts.summary: Recall words such as 'because', 'since', 'therefore' and 'thus' that signal reasons or conclusions.

concepts.name: Premises and conclusions
concepts.summary: Identify which statements in a short argument are the reasons offered and which is the point they are meant to support.

concepts.name: Arguments versus explanations
concepts.summary: Explain the difference between giving reasons to persuade someone a claim is true and explaining why something is the case.

concepts.name: Asking for evidence
concepts.summary: Understand that a claim needs support and that the person making it is expected to provide evidence.

concepts.name: Strong versus weak reasons
concepts.summary: Explain why a reason is stronger when it is relevant to the conclusion and backed by evidence rather than just repeated assertion.

misconceptions.text: Critical thinking means criticising or finding fault with everything.
If many people believe a claim or it is stated confidently, it counts as good evidence.
Every statement in an argument is a premise.

concepts.name: Extracting arguments from text
concepts.summary: Pick out premises and conclusion from a short everyday passage, ignoring rhetoric and filler, and lay them out in order.

concepts.name: Hidden assumptions
concepts.summary: Spot and state the unspoken premise that an everyday argument needs in order to get from its reasons to its conclusion.

concepts.name: Strawman fallacy
concepts.summary: Recognise when someone attacks a distorted or weakened version of an opponent's position instead of the real one.

concepts.name: Ad hominem fallacy
concepts.summary: Recognise when a claim is dismissed because of who said it rather than because of the reasons given.

concepts.name: Slippery slope fallacy
concepts.summary: Recognise arguments that claim one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without evidence for each link.

concepts.name: False dilemma
concepts.summary: Recognise when an argument presents only two options although others exist.

concepts.name: Correlation versus causation
concepts.summary: Explain that two things occurring together does not show that one causes the other.

misconceptions.text: If an argument commits a fallacy, its conclusion must be false.
Any personal remark about an opponent is an ad hominem fallacy.
Any argument that predicts bad consequences is a slippery slope fallacy.

concepts.name: Deductive versus inductive arguments
concepts.summary: Analyse whether an argument aims at guaranteeing its conclusion or only making it probable, and judge it by the matching standard.

concepts.name: Validity versus soundness
concepts.summary: Separate whether the conclusion follows from the premises from whether the premises are actually true.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.summary: Apply the idea that people favour evidence supporting existing beliefs to explain how a person's reasoning or information diet is skewed.

concepts.name: Common cognitive biases
concepts.summary: Identify biases such as anchoring, availability, and sunk cost in everyday judgments and decisions.

concepts.name: Source credibility assessment
concepts.summary: Weigh a source's expertise, evidence, incentives, and track record to judge how far to trust its claims.

concepts.name: Confounders and reverse causation
concepts.summary: Analyse a claimed causal link by looking for common causes, reversed direction, and coincidence.

concepts.name: Relevance and appeal fallacies
concepts.summary: Distinguish legitimate appeals to authority or popularity from fallacious ones, and spot red herrings that shift the topic.

concepts.name: Circular reasoning
concepts.summary: Detect arguments whose conclusion is already assumed in a premise and explain why that gives no real support.

misconceptions.text: A valid argument must have a true conclusion.
Being aware of biases means I am no longer affected by them.
Citing an authority is always a fallacy.

concepts.name: Evaluating evidence quality
concepts.summary: Judge how much a piece of evidence supports a claim by considering sample size, selection, controls, replication, and anecdote versus systematic data.

concepts.name: Base rates and statistical reasoning
concepts.summary: Analyse claims using base rates, proportions, and conditional probabilities rather than vivid cases.

concepts.name: Charitable argument reconstruction
concepts.summary: Rebuild an opponent's argument in its strongest plausible form before evaluating it.

concepts.name: Burden of proof allocation
concepts.summary: Judge who should carry the burden of proof in a dispute and detect attempts to shift it improperly.

concepts.name: Inference to the best explanation
concepts.summary: Compare rival explanations of the same evidence by fit, simplicity, scope, and testability and justify the preferred one.

concepts.name: Motivated reasoning and rhetoric
concepts.summary: Analyse how framing, emotional appeals, and identity-protective thinking shape both arguments and one's own judgment.

concepts.name: Judging fallacy accusations
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a suspected fallacy really undermines an argument in context, as slippery slope and authority appeals can sometimes be reasonable.

misconceptions.text: A large sample guarantees reliable evidence regardless of how it was collected.
Pointing out a fallacy settles the debate and proves the conclusion false.
Whoever doubts a claim never has to justify that doubt, so the burden always falls on the claimant.

concepts.name: Designing argument evaluation frameworks
concepts.summary: Create a reusable method for assessing arguments that weighs premise acceptability, relevance, sufficiency, and rebuttal across varied domains.

concepts.name: Calibrated belief updating
concepts.summary: Judge how strongly evidence should shift one's confidence and keep stated confidence matched to actual accuracy.

concepts.name: Debiasing strategies
concepts.summary: Design practical procedures, such as pre-mortems, devil's advocates, and outside-view checks, that reduce bias in individual and group decisions.

concepts.name: Limits of critical thinking
concepts.summary: Evaluate where critical analysis fails or misleads, including intellectual overconfidence, cynicism, expertise deference, and domain knowledge gaps.

concepts.name: Adversarial and disinformation analysis
concepts.summary: Assess deliberate manipulation tactics such as selective statistics, astroturfing, and coordinated misleading narratives and judge their likely effect.

concepts.name: Teaching and facilitating reasoning
concepts.summary: Create exercises and discussion formats that help others examine their own reasoning without triggering defensiveness.

misconceptions.text: Expert critical thinkers are immune to bias and manipulation.
Good critical thinking means distrusting all experts and institutions.
Being more confident in a conclusion shows better reasoning.
